text: One template with an invariant; lower_bound and upper_bound; real-number bisection.
lo hi x = 3: bad (a[i] < 3) | good (a[i] >= 3) invariant: a[lo] bad, a[hi] good; stop when hi = lo + 1 answer: hi = 1, the first good index

In a sorted array the test "a[i] ≥ x" is false for a prefix and true for the rest. Binary search finds the boundary by halving the range: look at the middle, keep the half that still contains the boundary. log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20 steps instead of 10⁶.
Use one template and its invariant always: lo is always bad (or −1), hi is always good (or n). The loop ends when they are neighbours, and hi is the first good index.

Templates mixing lo <= hi , mid + 1 and mid - 1 loop forever or miss by one when you change one detail. The hi - lo > 1 form never does: mid is always strictly between lo and hi.

title: The library versions: lower_bound and upper_bound

text: lower_bound(b, e, x) points to the first element ≥ x, upper_bound to the first element > x; both need sorted data and run in O(log n). Their difference counts the copies of x (P1102). The closest value to g is the element at lower_bound or the one just before it (P1678).
A continuous function that changes sign on [lo, hi] has a root there. Halving keeps the half where the sign still changes. Roots at least 1 apart means each unit interval holds at most one (P1024).
For real numbers, loop a fixed number of times (60 halvings shrink any range far below 10−9) instead of comparing with an epsilon. Interest rates (P1163) and times (P3743) are searched the same way.
Binary search over the answer with a check function.
check(H): green = enough wood, orange = not enough answer = the last green value, found in O(log range) checks
Binary search on the answer: when the question is "the largest (or smallest) x that works", and works(x) is monotone (if x works, every smaller x works too), search over x instead of over an array.
Each step costs one call to a check(x) function.
Recipe: (1) say what x is; (2) prove monotonicity in one sentence; (3) write check(x) , usually a greedy O(n) scan; (4) pick lo (surely works) and hi (surely fails) and run the template.

A higher saw gives less wood, so "enough wood" holds up to some height and fails above it (P1873). Longer pieces give fewer pieces (P2440). Both checks are one O(n) loop; with about 30 halvings the whole solution is O(n log range).

title: Maximise the minimum, minimise the maximum

text: "Make the smallest jump as large as possible" and "make the largest part as small as possible" are the classic signals for binary search on the answer. The check is a greedy pass: keep a stone only if it is far enough (P2678); start a new part only when the sum would exceed the cap (P1182). Road signs that shrink the longest gap (P3853) follow the same pattern.

Note which side is good in each problem: maximising keeps lo good and outputs lo ; minimising keeps hi good and outputs hi . Pick the starting lo and hi so the invariant is already true before the loop.
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Binary search needs a monotone test: false … false, true … true.
2. Template: lo always bad, hi always good; while (hi − lo > 1); answer hi (or lo).
3. mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 avoids overflow; mid is always strictly between lo and hi.
4. lower_bound: first ≥ x; upper_bound: first > x; difference = count of x.
5. Closest value: the lower_bound element or the one before it.
6. Real numbers: halve a fixed number of times (about 60), no epsilon needed.
7. Binary search on the answer: define x, prove monotone, write check(x), choose lo/hi.
8. "Maximise the minimum" / "minimise the maximum" → binary search on the answer.
9. The check is usually a greedy O(n) pass; total O(n log range).
